newsitem.title: USA: Armey reluctantly endorses China MFN.
newsitem.headline: Armey reluctantly endorses China MFN.

text.p: House of Representatives Majority Leader Dick Armey on Thursday reluctantly backed President Bill Clinton's decision to renew China's most favoured nation trade status.
But he said it was crucial to keep pressure on what he described as "a brutal dictatorship" in Beijing.

Armey, like other lawmakers, had been reconsidering his historical support for China's normal trade relations with the United States, in light of concern over China's human rights record and clampdowns on personal and economic freedoms.

But he finally decided late on Wednesday to back MFN status for China and try to effect change in China with other legislative initiatives such as denying visas to human rights violators, ending taxpayer subsidies of China and beefing up security arrangements in the western Pacific region.

"In my heart, I would like to oppose most favoured nation status for China as a way of expressing the deep repugnance I feel toward the tyranny of Beijing," the Texas Republican said in a foreign policy speech to the Nitze School of Advanced International Studies of Johns Hopkins University.

"But intellectually, I believe that continued normal trade relations are best for the people of China today and offer the best prospect for liberating them in years to come. I will vote to extend most favoured nation status for China."
Armey's decision will likely increase the chances the Congress will vote to renew China's MFN status.
The influential House Ways and Means Committee voted on Wednesday to back Clinton's decision to maintain normal U.S. trade relations with China and the full House will vote on the matter on Tuesday.
Clinton has been lobbying hard for China MFN renewal and on Thursday agreed to step up U.S. radio broadcasts to China, a move suggested by Armey, House Speaker Newt Gingrich and other lawmakers.
Clinton made the announcement in a letter to Gingrich, which was released in Denver, where the president is preparing to host a summit of the world's leading industrial nations.
Clinton has been an unabashed promoter of extending MFN status, saying it is the best way to remain engaged with the communist giant.

"Dealing with the MFN issue is only the first word in China policy, it must not be the last," Armey said in a text of his speech. "Congress should develop and pass China policy legislation later this year that will address our serious differences with China."

Representative Christopher Cox, a California Republican, and other House leaders, have been developing a comprehensive 10-bill package to "fill the void" caused by what they are calling Clinton's lack of leadership on U.S. policies toward China.
